questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of loose stool and fever. He was known to have bronchiectasis and required frequent admissions to hospital for chest infections. He had most recently been discharged 2 weeks earlier. He had severe abdominal pain and distension and was passing mucus per rectum. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 22.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL C-reactive protein 156 mg/L Serum creatinine 195μmol/L He was admitted and isolated in a single room.
questions.lead_in: What is the next step in his management?
questions.explanation: Oral vancomycin This patent has Clostridioides difficile secondary to recurrent courses of antibiotics and hospital exposure, and he has markers of severity with his raised white cell count and serum creatinine. He should be started on therapy as soon as possible with oral vancomycin, which achieves high levels within the bowel lumen compared to systemic therapy. Imaging should be arranged to ensure he does not have toxic megacolon, requiring a surgical opinion and intervention. Imaging may show signs of toxic megacolon or bowel perforation in addition to bowel mucosa and submucosa edema. If lower GI endoscopy is performed to exclude other causes, pseudomembranes may be visible as raised patches of yellow and white, 2 cm in diameter, on the mucosa, but endoscopy carries a risk of perforation and should not be performed early on in disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q19

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of watery diarrhea without noticing any blood in her stool. She had not been experiencing fevers or chills. She had not had any recent international travel but had received a course of ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection 2 months ago. Investigations: Total white cell count 14.1 ×109/L eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Stool Clostridioides difficile EIA for toxin A/B positive, GDH positive She responded well to treatment with oral vancomycin.

questions.model_answer: a) No. Infants and children up to 1-2 years of age are frequently asymptomatically colonized with toxigenic C. difficile, and the rate of stool positivity in young children with diarrhea is no higher than in those without; testing for CDI is not recommended in this age group and a positive assay should not be treated. b) Colonization is very common: when sampled monthly over the first year of life essentially all infants are colonized at some point with toxigenic and/or nontoxigenic strains. c) Beyond age 3 years the colonization rate resembles that of adults (<3%).

questions.model_answer: a) Fidaxomicin is a macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase, blocking transcription. b) (1) Minimal systemic absorption with high intraluminal/fecal concentrations delivered to the colon; (2) narrow spectrum with relatively sparing effect on the normal gut anaerobic microbiota. c) Comparable cure to vancomycin but a significantly lower rate of subsequent recurrence (e.g., ~20% vs ~35% with vancomycin).
questions.beyond_mandell: The mechanism of action (macrolide/macrocyclic class, RNA polymerase inhibition) and the minimal-absorption/microbiota-sparing pharmacology are established drug facts; this chapter documents the recurrence benefit but does not spell out the mechanism or PK in detail.

cohort_answer.text: Inhibits RNA polymerase sigma subunit resulting in inhibition of protein synthesis and cell death; bactericidal. || Minimal systemic absorption – distribution mainly to GI tract; No dose adjustment needed for renal or hepatic impairment; Limited activity against bowel flora. || Decreased relapse rates compared to vanco/metro. Hypervirulent strain NAP1/B1/027 – fidaxomicin works better on this strain.

questions.model_answer: a) A tetracycline (e.g., doxycycline)-tetracyclines are in the lower-risk category for CDI. b) Clindamycin-classified as highest risk for CDI. c) (1) Number of antibiotics given (risk rises with more agents); (2) duration/days of antibiotic therapy (risk rises with longer courses). (Also relevant: advanced patient age, prior/duration of hospitalization.) d) (1) Reduce overuse of antimicrobials, especially restricting high-risk agents (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins); (2) implement antimicrobial stewardship interventions, which reduce CDI incidence (~32% in meta-analysis).

cohort_answer.text:
Most effective oral treatment causing least diarrhea: Tetracyclines (also macrolides, narrow spectrum beta lactams)
Most effective oral treatment causing most C. diff diarrhea: Clindamycin
Two other factors: Advanced age; Duration of hospitalization; Prolonged exposure to antibiotics
Two antimicrobial measures to limit C diff risk: Minimize the frequency and duration of high-risk antibiotic therapy and the number of antibiotic agents prescribed, to reduce CDI risk (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). Implement an antibiotic stewardship program (good practice recommendation). Antibiotics to be targeted should be based on the local epidemiology and the C. difficile strains present. Restriction of fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, and cephalosporins (except for surgical antibiotic prophylaxis) should be considered (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). No evidence for d/c PPI or probiotics

questions.question: C. difficile scenarios: an 8-month-old infant with non-severe diarrhea; a 14-year-old male with a second recurrence; a 77-year-old female with a first non-severe episode; a 50-year-old male with pseudomembranous colitis developing ileus; a 48-year-old male with a second recurrence.
questions.question_raw: C difficile scenarios: 8mo old infant with non-severe diarrhea; 14yo M with second recurrence; 77yo F with first episode non-severe diarrhea; 50yo M with pseudomembranous colitis and developing ileus; 48yo M with second recurrence.

parts.text: For each scenario, state the appropriate management.

parts_raw.text: For each scenario, state the appropriate management

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old, non-severe: do not test/treat-infants are frequently asymptomatically colonized; a positive assay does not constitute CDI and no antibiotic is indicated. b) 14-year-old, second recurrence: vancomycin taper-and-pulse regimen, or vancomycin followed by rifaximin, or fidaxomicin; fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) after adequate antibiotic treatment of at least two recurrences. c) 77-year-old, first non-severe episode: oral vancomycin 125 mg PO qid x10 d or fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x10 d (metronidazole only if these are unavailable/contraindicated). d) 50-year-old, PMC with ileus (fulminant): oral/NG vancomycin 500 mg qid PLUS IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h, add vancomycin retention enema (500 mg in 100 mL saline q6h) if complete ileus, with early surgical consultation for possible colectomy/diverting ileostomy. e) 48-year-old, second recurrence: vancomycin taper-and-pulse, or vancomycin then rifaximin, or fidaxomicin; consider FMT.

questions.question: Clostridioides difficile testing.

parts.text: Describe the components of C. difficile testing.
What is the limitation to NAAT testing clinically?

parts_raw.text: Describe the components of C. diff testing
What is the limitation to NAAT testing clinically?

questions.model_answer: a) Tests fall into those detecting the organism/toxin genes versus those detecting free toxin: (1) glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) EIA-detects organism (toxigenic and nontoxigenic), high sensitivity/NPV, a screening step; (2) toxin A/B EIA-detects free toxin, specific but relatively insensitive; (3) NAAT (PCR or LAMP)-detects toxin gene, most sensitive rapid single test; plus reference standards cell cytotoxicity assay and toxigenic culture. These are combined in multistep algorithms: two-step (GDH + toxin EIA) and three-step (GDH + toxin EIA with NAAT arbitration of discrepant results). b) NAAT detects the presence of the toxin gene, not toxin in stool, so used alone it cannot distinguish true CDI from asymptomatic colonization with diarrhea from another cause; it therefore overdiagnoses CDI (apparent rates rise ~50%), and NAAT-alone-positive/toxin-negative patients have lower rates of complications and death.

questions.question: Explain the C. difficile multi-test algorithm and the limitations of NAAT-only testing.
questions.question_raw: C diff: multi test algorithm explain, limitations to NAAT only testing.

parts.text: Explain the C. difficile multi-test algorithm and the limitations of NAAT-only testing.

parts_raw.text: C diff: multi test algorithm explain, limitations to NAAT only testing.

questions.model_answer: Multistep algorithm: begin with a sensitive screen-GDH EIA (or GDH/toxin combination), using its high negative predictive value to report 80-95% of specimens as negative rapidly. In the two-step algorithm GDH is paired with a toxin A/B EIA; when these are discrepant (13-19% of tests) a third step uses NAAT to arbitrate (three-step algorithm), giving rapid turnaround at lower cost than testing every specimen by NAAT. NAAT-only limitation: NAAT detects the toxin gene (i.e., presence of toxigenic organism), not free toxin in stool; used alone it cannot separate true CDI from colonized patients with diarrhea from another cause, causing overdiagnosis (~50% rise in apparent CDI) and detecting patients with milder disease/lower complication and mortality rates.

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old: do not treat-infants are commonly colonized and a positive test does not mean CDI; confirm true infection and provide supportive care only. b) 13-year-old, second recurrence: fecal microbiota transplantation (appropriate after adequate antibiotic treatment of >=2 recurrences); alternatively vancomycin taper-and-pulse or vancomycin followed by rifaximin. c) 50-year-old, fulminant with ileus: oral/NG vancomycin 500 mg qid PLUS IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h, add rectal vancomycin enema if complete ileus, with early surgical consult. d) 40-year-old, first non-severe: fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x10 d (or oral vancomycin 125 mg qid x10 d).

cohort_answer.text: 8 month old: ensure true C. diff (infants <12 months often colonized); if treated, can use same regimen as adults (vancomycin) with adjusted dose. 13yo second recurrence: strongest recommendation/evidence for fecal transplant; otherwise treated similarly to first recurrence (pulse/tapering vancomycin); option to use rifaximin for 20 days after initial vancomycin (fidaxomicin never gets a taper). 50yo fulminant colitis and ileus: Vancomycin PO + Metronidazole (Flagyl) IV. 40yo first non-severe episode: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days; Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x10 days; or metronidazole as a weak alternative x10 days at TID dosing.

questions.model_answer: a) Two-tier (two-step) testing: a sensitive initial screen with GDH EIA (detects organism; high NPV), paired with a toxin A/B EIA (detects free toxin; specific). Rationale: GDH rapidly and cheaply rules out 80-95% of negatives while the toxin EIA confirms toxigenic active infection; discrepant results can be arbitrated by NAAT (three-step), balancing sensitivity, specificity, cost, and turnaround. b) NAAT detects the toxin gene, not free toxin, so alone it cannot distinguish CDI from colonized patients whose diarrhea has another cause, overdiagnosing CDI (~50% apparent increase) and capturing milder/lower-risk patients. c) Examples dosable with thrice-weekly hemodialysis sessions: (1) vancomycin IV; (2) cefazolin IV; (3) daptomycin IV.
questions.beyond_mandell: Part (c) on intermittent hemodialysis antibiotic dosing (vancomycin, cefazolin, daptomycin given with dialysis) is not covered in this chapter; answer drawn from standard dialysis-dosing references.

parts.text: Name two other causes of antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

parts_raw.text: A) What are 2 other causes of antibiotic associated diarrhea
B) If the patient has C. diff, list 2 reasons why the initial testing was negative?
C) IPAC measures for preventing horizontal transmission of C. diff?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Overgrowth of other enteric pathogens when normal flora is disrupted (e.g., Klebsiella oxytoca, Clostridium perfringens, Staphylococcus aureus). (2) Functional/osmotic diarrhea from antibiotic-induced disruption of the microbiota (reduced carbohydrate fermentation and short-chain fatty acid production) and direct antibiotic effects on motility. b) (1) Infection with an A-/B+ strain that produces only toxin B — the toxin A EIA misses these (this is why the toxin A-only EIA became obsolete). (2) Poor sensitivity of toxin EIA (toxin A/B EIA is relatively insensitive versus cell cytotoxicity assay and toxigenic culture), so low-level toxin falls below the detection threshold. c) Contact precautions (gowns and gloves for all patient/environment contact); single-patient room with dedicated noncritical equipment (thermometer, stethoscope); hand hygiene — gloves required because alcohol sanitizers do not remove spores, with soap and water preferred; sporicidal disinfectant (bleach/peracetic acid) for daily and terminal room cleaning; and antimicrobial stewardship to reduce high-risk agents.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific non-C. difficile AAD pathogens (K. oxytoca, C. perfringens, S. aureus) are cited only in this chapter's reference list, not its main text; standard AAD knowledge.

cohort_answer.text:
Post-infectious IBD: disruption of microbiota with antibiotics reduces carbohydrate digestion, reduces short chain fatty acid production - causes osmotic diarrhea - reduces bile acid breakdown - more diarrhea. Other enteric pathogens: disrupted normal flora allows overgrowth of organisms that induce diarrhea: C. diff, C perfringens, S aureus, Candida, K oxytoca, Salmonella. Direct effect of antibiotic: occurs in 5-30% of pts on antibiotics (RF: age>65, immunosuppressed, ICU, prolonged hospitalization); AmoxClav can stimulate bowel motility; Erythromycin causes accelerated gastric emptying; Penicillins cause segmental colitis
Variant of toxin B that produces Toxin B only; Low level toxin production below threshold of EIA Detection; Delay between stool collection and delivery to lab – toxin degrades at room temp and may be undetectable within 2h (should be stored at 4C if delay in transport)
Isolation: Private room with dedicated toilet; Contact precautions until 48h after diarrhea resolved. HCW: contact precautions, hand hygiene (soap + water preferred). Patients: encourage hand hygiene. Equipment: Disposable equipment or thoroughly disinfect with sporicidal agent. Room cleaning: terminal room clean with sporicidal agent, daily cleaning with sporicidal agent. ASP

questions.question: Clostridioides difficile.

parts.text: List four strategies that can be implemented by infection prevention and control to control the spread of Clostridioides difficile in institutions.

parts_raw.text: A. Four strategies that can be implemented by infection prevention & control to control spread of C. difficile in institutions.

questions.model_answer:
(1) Contact precautions (gown and gloves) in a single room with a dedicated toilet or commode for all suspected and confirmed cases, continued until at least 48 hours after diarrhea resolves.
(2) Hand hygiene with soap and water after contact with the patient or environment (alcohol does not kill spores), and dedicated or single-use patient equipment.
(3) Daily and terminal environmental cleaning with a sporicidal agent (chlorine-based, e.g. 1000-5000 ppm), with auditing of cleaning quality.
(4) Antimicrobial stewardship to reduce high-risk agents (fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, clindamycin), coupled with laboratory-based surveillance, case-rate feedback to units, prompt testing of patients with diarrhea, and staff/visitor education.

cohort_answer.text: Contact isolation with private toilet for known or suspected cases; Hand hygiene soap and water for visible soiling; Daily and Terminal sporicidal cleaning of pt room; Use antibiotics judiciously; Surveillance

questions.model_answer:
(1) Contact precautions (gown and gloves for all room entry) with placement in a single room with a dedicated toilet.

questions.question: Management of a patient with severe Clostridioides difficile colitis.

parts.text: Management of a patient with severe Clostridioides difficile colitis.

parts_raw.text: Management of a patient with severe C. difficile colitis.

questions.model_answer: Severe CDI (WBC >15,000/µL or serum creatinine >1.5x baseline): vancomycin 125 mg PO qid x 10 days (preferred agent), OR fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x 10 days. Metronidazole is no longer recommended for severe disease. Monitor clinical response daily; successful treatment is judged by symptom resolution, not by repeat stool testing (test-of-cure should not be done).

cohort_answer.text: For initial episode of severe disease: Vancomycin 125mg orally 4 times daily for 10 days, or Fidaxomicin 200mg orally twice daily for 10 days. For initial episode of fulminant disease: Vancomycin 500mg orally or by NG tube 4x daily plus Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h. Consider rectal vancomycin instillation if complete ileus.

(2) Functional/osmotic diarrhea from antibiotic-induced microbiota disruption (reduced carbohydrate fermentation/SCFA production) and direct antibiotic motility effects (e.g., macrolides as motilin agonists, clavulanate stimulating bowel motility).
questions.beyond_mandell: Non-C. difficile AAD pathogens appear only in this chapter's reference list; standard antibiotic-associated diarrhea knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: Post-infectious IBS from changes to fermentation leading to osmotic diarrhea; Molecular mimicry - direct effect from abx; Clavulin - stimulates bowel motility; Erythromycin - stimulates gastric emptying; Overgrowth of other gut bacteria. [Background: antibiotics reduce fecal anaerobes; erythromycin/macrolides are motilin-receptor agonists; clavulanate stimulates small-bowel motility]

parts.text: If the patient had Clostridioides difficile-associated disease, list two reasons why the initial testing was negative.

parts_raw.text: B) If the patient had CDAD, list 2 reasons why the initial testing was negative?

questions.model_answer: (1) Infection with an A-/B+ strain producing only toxin B — a toxin A EIA misses these organisms (the reason the toxin A-only EIA was abandoned). (2) Low sensitivity of toxin EIA (toxin A/B EIA is relatively insensitive versus cell cytotoxicity assay and toxigenic culture), so low-level toxin is below the detection threshold.

cohort_answer.text: Variant of toxin B that produces Toxin B only; Low level toxin production below threshold of EIA detection; Delay between stool collection and delivery to lab - toxin degrades at room temp and may be undetectable within 2h (should be stored at 4C if delay in transport)

parts.text: Infection prevention and control measures for preventing horizontal transmission of Clostridioides difficile.

parts_raw.text: C) IPAC measures for preventing horizontal transmission of C diff

questions.model_answer:
(1) Isolation: single room with a dedicated toilet/commode, contact precautions initiated empirically at the time of testing and continued until at least 48 hours after diarrhea resolves (longer during outbreaks or until discharge).
(2) Healthcare workers: gown and gloves for every room entry; hand hygiene with soap and water after care because alcohol does not inactivate spores.
(3) Patients and visitors: instruct on hand hygiene, restrict movement off the unit, and limit visitors with education on PPE.
(4) Equipment: dedicated or single-use thermometers, stethoscopes and commodes; disinfect any shared items with a sporicidal agent.
(5) Environment: daily and terminal cleaning with a chlorine-based sporicidal disinfectant, with audit of cleaning adequacy.
(6) System measures: antimicrobial stewardship to limit high-risk agents, surveillance with unit-level rate feedback, and prompt testing of all patients with unexplained diarrhea (a negative toxin EIA is insensitive — repeat with NAAT/GDH algorithm rather than assuming the patient is not infected).

cohort_answer.text: Isolation: private room with dedicated toilet, contact precautions until 48h after diarrhea resolved. HCW: contact precautions, hand hygiene (soap and water preferred). Patients: encourage hand hygiene. Equipment: disposable or thoroughly disinfect with sporicidal agent. Room cleaning: terminal clean and daily clean with sporicidal agent. ASP.

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old: no CDI treatment/testing indicated — children under 1-2 years are frequently asymptomatically colonized with toxigenic C. difficile and testing is not recommended; investigate other causes of diarrhea. b) 13-year-old, second recurrence (>one recurrence): vancomycin taper-and-pulse regimen, OR vancomycin 10 days followed by rifaximin, OR fidaxomicin, OR fecal microbiota transplantation (weight-based pediatric dosing). c) 50-year-old, fulminant (fevers, ileus, shock): vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG qid PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h, with vancomycin 500 mg in 100 mL saline per rectum q6h if complete ileus; early surgical consult for possible colectomy/ileostomy. d) 45-year-old, second recurrence (>one recurrence): vancomycin taper-and-pulse, OR vancomycin 125 mg PO qid x 10 d then rifaximin 400 mg PO tid x 20 d, OR fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x 10 d, OR fecal microbiota transplantation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Pediatric weight-based dosing is not specified in this chapter (adult doses given); peds dosing from IDSA/guideline sources.

cohort_answer.text: 8 month old: No treatment indicated unless other causes ruled out; if treating, Metronidazole 30mg/kg/day in 4 doses for 10-14 days. 13M second recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days or tapered. 50yo fevers/ileus/shock (fulminant): Vancomycin 500mg PO QID + Metronidazole 500mg IV Q8 + rectal instillation of vancomycin. 45yo second recurrence: Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days OR Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days followed by prolonged taper OR Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days followed by rifaximin 400mg TID x20 days.

parts.text: Describe two-tier testing and its rationale.
Why may NAAT not be a good stand-alone test?

parts_raw.text: Describe two tier testing and its rationale
Why may NAAT not be a great stand alone test?

questions.model_answer: a) Two-step algorithm: initial EIA for glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH, a common antigen present on all C. difficile, toxigenic and nontoxigenic — high sensitivity, high negative predictive value, lower specificity) paired with an EIA for toxins A/B (high specificity, low sensitivity). Concordant results (both positive or both negative) are reported directly; discrepant results (13%-19%) are arbitrated by NAAT (three-step algorithm). Rationale: GDH rapidly and sensitively rules out C. difficile in 80%-95% of specimens, the toxin EIA confirms toxin production, and NAAT resolves discrepancies — retaining sensitivity and specificity while limiting the cost of testing every specimen by NAAT. b) NAAT detects the toxin gene, not toxin in stool, so it identifies toxigenic organism presence like a toxigenic culture but cannot distinguish active CDI from asymptomatic colonization. Because it is so sensitive, used alone it overdiagnoses (apparent CDI rates rise ~50%); NAAT+/toxin- patients have significantly lower mortality, ICU admission, and colectomy rates than NAAT+/toxin+ patients, so NAAT-alone may capture colonized patients whose diarrhea has another cause.

cohort_answer.text: Step 1 - testing for both glutamate dehydrogenase antigen (found on all C difficile isolates) and toxin A/B using enzyme linked immunoassay: GDH - high sensitivity, lower specificity; Toxins - high specificity, low sensitivity. Step 2 - NAAT testing to confirm presence of C diff toxin gene specific to toxigenic strains (highly sensitive so can rule out infection if negative but does not discriminate between toxin producing and non-toxin producing, colonizing C difficile). Want NAAT testing to follow up if discordant results between GDH and toxin antigens - more expensive but more specific for toxigenic strains, and sensitive

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old: no CDI treatment or testing — children <1-2 years are routinely colonized with toxigenic C. difficile and stool positivity does not indicate disease; evaluate for other causes. b) 13-year-old, second recurrence: vancomycin taper-and-pulse regimen (weight-based pediatric dosing). c) 50-year-old, fulminant (fevers, ileus, shock): vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG qid PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h, plus rectal vancomycin (500 mg in 100 mL saline q6h) if complete ileus; early surgical consultation. d) 45-year-old, second recurrence: vancomycin 125 mg PO qid x 10 d followed by rifaximin 400 mg PO tid x 20 d (alternatively fidaxomicin 200 mg PO bid x 10 d, or fecal microbiota transplantation after at least two recurrences).
questions.beyond_mandell: Pediatric weight-based dosing is not specified in this chapter; peds dosing from guideline sources.

cohort_answer.text:
8 month old: No treatment indicated (should not test in those <2, as routine colonizer that doesn't cause disease). [Note: less toxin receptors in neonatal colons, maternal Ab, different microbiome.]
13M second recurrence: Vancomycin 40mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses (10mg/kg/dose, max 125mg/dose) x10-14 days, then 10mg/kg/dose BID x7 days, then 10mg/kg/dose once daily x7 days, then 10mg/kg/dose q2-3 days x2-8 weeks.
50yo fevers, ileus, shock: Vancomycin 500mg PO/NG QID + Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h + rectal instillation of vancomycin (if ileus present).
45yo second recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO qid x10 days followed by Rifaximin 400mg TID x20 days; OR Vancomycin 125mg PO qid x10-14 days, then BID x7 days, then once daily x7 days, then 125mg PO q2-3 days x2-8 weeks; OR Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x10 days; OR Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x5 days then 200mg PO EOD x20 days; OR Fecal Microbiota Transplantation.
